power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Proactive Academic Stress Screening in Education: NPRO-8 Core Mental Fitness Screening

author.affiliation:
Erasmus University Medical Center
								the Netherlands Rotgans Research
								
									Singapore

text.text: Academic stress is a longstanding concern in education, with evidence linking it to examination difficulties, disrupted sleep, and poorer wellbeing.
A student support pathway that depends on students requesting help or showing visible deterioration risks intervening only after difficulties have affected daily functioning.
This paper proposes NPRO-8 Core as a new approach to proactive, objective assessment of stress-related functioning in students.
Its preventive rationale is to create opportunities for recognition and support before difficulties escalate.
A two-tier pathway combines brief screening offered across an institution with targeted functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) assessment during structured cognitive tasks.
The assessment considers Stress Load, Recovery Capacity, and Functional Impact, with repeated measurements intended to support review over time.
Questionnaires provide access to students' experiences; physiological and behavioural measures add a complementary perspective that does not depend solely on recognizing and reporting distress.
The proposed contribution is to integrate these sources into a proactive student support pathway.
Drawing on the preventive logic of physical-health screening, the framework links measurement to timely review and appropriate action.
Academic stress is a persistent and increasingly pressing problem in education.
Students face demands to master growing bodies of knowledge, meet competing deadlines, and demonstrate their ability through examinations that can shape subsequent educational opportunities.

When these demands exceed their capacity to cope and recover, the consequences extend beyond feeling under pressure: learning, examination performance, sleep, and psychological wellbeing can all be affected.
This concern begins well before university.
International monitoring shows that schoolwork pressure increased between 2014 and 2022, with particularly marked increases among adolescent girls (WHO Regional Office for Europe, 2024a).

Academic stress therefore demands sustained attention throughout education, including middle and high school, where students are developing the cognitive and emotional resources needed to manage academic demands.
The scale and direction of this problem are evident in the Health Behaviour in School-aged Children study.
Across participating countries and regions in Europe, central Asia, and Canada, 63% of 15year-old girls reported feeling pressured by schoolwork in 2022, compared with 54% in 2018.
Among boys of the same age, the proportion increased from 40% to 43% (WHO Regional Office for Europe, 2024b).
These findings show that academic pressure is both widespread and increasing during a consequential period of students' development.
The problem also continues into college and university.

In the 2024 American College Health Association survey, involving 103,639 students at 154 US institutions, 36.8% reported that stress had adversely affected their academic performance during the preceding year (American College Health Association, 2024).
Together, these findings establish a substantial educational concern spanning school and postsecondary study.
The consequences for achievement have been documented across decades of research.

In a synthesis of 238 studies, von der Embse et al. (2018) found that test anxiety was negatively associated with educational outcomes including standardized test performance, entrance examinations, and grade point average.
text.formatted: In a synthesis of 238 studies, von der Embse et al. <ref type="bibr">(2018)</ref> found that test anxiety was negatively associated with educational outcomes including standardized test performance, entrance examinations, and grade point average.

text.text: Evidence from secondary education reinforces this relationship: von der Embse and Witmer (2014) found that test anxiety predicted statewide assessment performance among 1,134 eleventhgrade students after accounting for other predictors, including grade point average.

Physiological research points in the same direction. Heissel et al. (2021) linked cortisol responses during high-stakes testing to poorer-than-expected performance among students in grades 3-8, while Ng et al. (2003) found that higher pre-examination stress and cortisol were associated with lower examination scores in graduate students.
text.formatted: Physiological research points in the same direction. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Heissel et al. (2021)</ref> linked cortisol responses during high-stakes testing to poorer-than-expected performance among students in grades 3-8, while <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Ng et al. (2003)</ref> found that higher pre-examination stress and cortisol were associated with lower examination scores in graduate students.

text.text: The convergence of reported anxiety, physiological responses, and academic outcomes makes stress relevant to how educators understand students' performance.
These relationships matter because an examination result can influence access to later courses, progression, and educational choices.
A student who struggles to retrieve familiar material under pressure may achieve a result that does not fully reflect their preparation.

Difficulties can also accumulate across a programme of study. Vaez and Laflamme (2008), following 1,127 Swedish university students, found that stress associated with difficulties coping academically and demands for study support was related to poorer degree completion outcomes.
text.formatted: Difficulties can also accumulate across a programme of study. <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Vaez and Laflamme (2008)</ref>, following 1,127 Swedish university students, found that stress associated with difficulties coping academically and demands for study support was related to poorer degree completion outcomes.

text.text: Academic stress consequently deserves attention both during individual assessments and across students' longer educational trajectories.
Psychological mechanisms help explain why stress can interfere with learning and performance.
Working memory enables students to retain and manipulate information while completing a task.
Cognitive flexibility allows them to change strategies when a solution fails or a question introduces a new requirement.
A meta-analysis of experimental research found that acute stress impaired both working memory and cognitive flexibility (Shields et al., 2016).
text.formatted: A meta-analysis of experimental research found that acute stress impaired both working memory and cognitive flexibility <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Shields et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: In educational terms, these processes allow a student to keep track of intermediate steps in a mathematics problem, integrate information across a passage, or abandon an ineffective approach.
When these functions are disrupted, a student may lose their place in a calculation, struggle to connect ideas, or persist with the wrong strategy despite having the relevant knowledge.
Memory retrieval provides a further explanation.
Stress affects different stages of memory processing differently, and stress at retrieval can make previously learned information harder to access (Vogel & Schwabe, 2016).
text.formatted: Stress affects different stages of memory processing differently, and stress at retrieval can make previously learned information harder to access <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Vogel & Schwabe, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: This helps explain the familiar experience of a student knowing material during revision but struggling to recall it during an examination.
The educational concern is therefore not simply how much a student has studied, but whether they can use that knowledge effectively under demand.
It also explains the value of considering cognitive functioning alongside reported stress.

Stress-related difficulties extend into the periods in which students should recover. Zunhammer et al. (2014) followed 150 university students before, during, and after examinations and documented increased perceived stress alongside poorer sleep quality, reduced time in bed, and insomnia symptoms during the examination period.
text.formatted: Stress-related difficulties extend into the periods in which students should recover. <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Zunhammer et al. (2014)</ref> followed 150 university students before, during, and after examinations and documented increased perceived stress alongside poorer sleep quality, reduced time in bed, and insomnia symptoms during the examination period.

text.text: A student who extends revision late into the night and then struggles to settle has less opportunity to recover before the next day's demands.
This makes recovery an essential part of understanding how students sustain their functioning across repeated periods of academic pressure.
Visible achievement does not always reveal these difficulties.

Benítez-Agudelo et al. (2025) followed 115 psychology students across a semester and found that academic performance improved while sleep, anxiety, depressive symptoms, and physiological indicators showed deterioration.
This pattern is particularly relevant to early identification: maintaining good grades does not necessarily mean that a student is coping well.
Attention to stress load and recovery can therefore address concerns that an exclusive focus on academic results may overlook.

There is also evidence that appropriate support can make a difference. Huntley et al. (2019) synthesized 44 randomized controlled trials involving 2,209 test-anxious university students and found that interventions reduced test anxiety and improved academic performance.
text.formatted: There is also evidence that appropriate support can make a difference. <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Huntley et al. (2019)</ref> synthesized 44 randomized controlled trials involving 2,209 test-anxious university students and found that interventions reduced test anxiety and improved academic performance.

text.text: These findings provide a practical reason to identify difficulties and connect students with support.
The central educational challenge is to create that opportunity early enough, before persistent strain develops into more substantial disruption of learning or wellbeing.

This leads to the question addressed in the present paper: how can education move toward proactive assessment of stress-related functioning, rather than depend primarily on students seeking help or showing visible deterioration?
A service that depends on students presenting themselves for help requires them to recognize a difficulty, decide it warrants attention, and disclose it.
Evidence suggests that this route will not reach everyone. Ebert et al. (2019) surveyed 13,984 first-year college students in eight countries.
text.formatted: Evidence suggests that this route will not reach everyone. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Ebert et al. (2019)</ref> surveyed 13,984 first-year college students in eight countries.

text.text: Only 24.6% said they would definitely seek treatment for a future emotional problem.
Among those who did not express that definite intention, 56.4% preferred to manage the problem themselves and 48.0% preferred talking to friends or relatives.
These are intentions and stated barriers, not observed rates of treatment uptake, but they expose a weakness in relying exclusively on spontaneous help-seeking.
Similarly, a referral triggered by falling grades, repeated absence, or an acute crisis begins after an adverse consequence has become visible.
In the familiar analogy, this resembles an ambulance waiting at the bottom of a cliff.
Crisis services remain essential, but prevention requires opportunities to identify vulnerability earlier.
Moving towards proactive support therefore requires more than encouraging students to ask for help.
Institutions need planned opportunities to assess stress-related difficulties before those difficulties become visible through declining performance or crisis.
This creates a measurement question: what can be assessed, and how can the resulting information guide timely support?
Blood-pressure screening illustrates the logic.
In adults, identifying hypertension and linking it to appropriate treatment can reduce cardiovascular events (US Preventive Services Task Force, 2021).
Assessment need not wait until a heart attack has occurred.
Its value comes from identifying actionable risk and responding in time, rather than merely producing a measurement.
The same principle provides a rationale for proactive stress assessment in education.
If support is to begin earlier, institutions need information that can be gathered before a student requests help or experiences an obvious educational setback.
Measurement becomes the link between the ambition to prevent deterioration and the decision to offer support.
The analogy concerns this sequence of assessment and action; the educational application requires measures suited to students and the demands they encounter.
Self-report questionnaires provide a practical starting point.
Offered routinely, they can reach students who have not approached a teacher, counsellor, or student support service.
They also capture experiences that cannot be inferred from examination results or classroom behaviour alone.
However, they depend on students recognizing, interpreting, and reporting their experience.
Where assessment begins only after a student discloses a problem, the institution remains dependent on the same helpseeking process that proactive support is intended to move beyond.
The measurement need is therefore broader than asking students how stressed they feel.
It includes examining how they respond to demands, how they recover afterwards, and whether their functioning changes under pressure.
For example, a student may continue to achieve good marks while finding sustained concentration increasingly demanding.

A questionnaire can establish how that student experiences the situation; structured physiological and behavioural assessment can add a different source of information about their response during a task.
This calls for an approach that connects accessible screening with more focused objective assessment.
Broad screening can identify students for follow-up, while targeted measurement can examine their responses to standardized demands in greater detail.
Bringing these sources together would give educators a basis for discussing support before visible deterioration becomes the principal signal that something is wrong.
NPRO-8 Core is proposed as a response to this measurement need.
It is a structured assessment approach that combines functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) with cognitive tasks to examine stress-related functioning.
During the tasks, fNIRS records optical signals used to estimate changes in oxygenated and deoxygenated haemoglobin, providing information about cortical haemodynamic responses.
Behavioural measures, including accuracy and response speed, show how the student performs under the same demands.
Together, these measurements complement the student's account with observations that do not depend solely on self-report.
The NPRO-8 theoretical framework organizes this information around three dimensions: Stress Load, Recovery Capacity, and Functional Impact (Rotgans, 2026).
text.formatted: The NPRO-8 theoretical framework organizes this information around three dimensions: Stress Load, Recovery Capacity, and Functional Impact <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Rotgans, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These dimensions address related educational questions: how demanding is the student's response, how readily does the student recover, and how is functioning affected during cognitive activity?
The following section explains each dimension and its relationship to the assessment tasks.
In the proposed two-tier pathway, a brief initial screen creates an opportunity to reach students across an institution.
Students identified for follow-up can then receive the more focused NPRO-8 Core assessment, with results considered alongside their experience and educational context.
Repeated review connects assessment to support over time.
The contribution proposed here is the integration of physiological and behavioural measurement into this proactive educational pathway.

Physiological stress measurement already has an established research history in students (Heissel et al., 2021); NPRO-8 Core brings that measurement perspective into a structured model of screening, targeted assessment, and follow-up.
text.formatted: Physiological stress measurement already has an established research history in students <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Heissel et al., 2021)</ref>; NPRO-8 Core brings that measurement perspective into a structured model of screening, targeted assessment, and follow-up.

text.text: Stress Load concerns burden or regulatory demand during baseline and task conditions.
In education, it asks whether a student shows a response pattern consistent with unusually demanding engagement.
The assessment considers this response alongside the student's reported experience and educational context.
Educationally, this raises the question of how readily students settle after demanding activity.
Withinsession recovery provides a focused observation that can be considered alongside the student's experience of rest and recovery in everyday life.
Functional Impact concerns accuracy, response speed, stability, and physiological response during cognitive demands.

These measures describe how a student functions during the assessment and provide a basis for discussing difficulties with attention, interference, or changing task requirements in educational settings.

The theoretical framework describes eight probes: Baseline Load, Vigilance/Endurance, Recovery Under Vigilance, Conflict Processing, Recovery After Conflict, Cognitive Flexibility, Strategic Integration, and Uncertainty Tolerance.
The stimulus materials illustrate related demands involving response inhibition, interference, rule changes, integration of instructions, and unexpected feedback.
The probes provide structured opportunities to observe responses to different demands and the recovery periods that follow them.
Keeping the three dimensions distinct helps organize the discussion of support.
Preserved task accuracy alongside a changed physiological response, for example, can prompt a discussion of the effort involved in maintaining performance.
A slower return towards baseline can draw attention to recovery.
Considering the dimensions together encourages a fuller account of the student's functioning than performance alone.

The proactive element begins with who is invited and when: screening is offered to the eligible student population at planned times, with appropriate consent, rather than being triggered solely by a complaint or a fall in performance.
Follow-up intervals should be specified and evaluated.
An institution-wide invitation does not mean that every student receives a brain assessment.
Figure 1 illustrates the two-tier pathway.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref> illustrates the two-tier pathway.

text.text: In the proposed school-based pathway (Figure 1), Tier 1 consists of a brief digital screen designed to take approximately two to three minutes and to be offered across an institution.
text.formatted: In the proposed school-based pathway (Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>), Tier 1 consists of a brief digital screen designed to take approximately two to three minutes and to be offered across an institution.

text.text: This first tier provides a practical way to identify reported difficulties and prioritize follow-up without requiring a physiological session for every student.
The screen combines self-reported experience and task performance.
The framework uses green, amber, and red categories.
For research and implementation, these should represent provisional follow-up priorities rather than established probabilities of illness.
Green would lead to routine support and opportunities for later review.
Amber would prompt contextual review and possible repeat screening.
Red would prompt timely personal contact and consideration of further assessment.
Students must retain access to support through self-referral, family concerns, or staff observations regardless of their category.
Otherwise, a brief screen could become a barrier for students whose difficulties it misses.
Immediate concerns about safety or serious distress should enter the institution's existing safeguarding or clinical referral pathway without waiting for Tier 2.
Students selected for follow-up would be offered NPRO-8 Core assessment, subject to consent and contextual review.
It is an approximately ten-minute assessment using fNIRS during structured tasks.
Scheduling should also allow for explanation, sensor fitting, signal checks, cleaning, and discussion of results.
Tier 2 would examine task responses and recovery alongside behavioural performance and the student's account.
A trained reviewer would consider whether the combined information suggests a need for further assessment, a change in support, or monitoring.
The physiological result should not automatically override the student's experience.
Disagreement between sources is itself a reason to investigate context.
The central sequence is: offer broad screening, review follow-up priorities, undertake targeted assessment where useful, agree support, and review progress.
The two tiers describe assessment intensity; they do not replace the institution's wider support system.
The framework also incorporates repeated sessions and trajectories for the three dimensions (Figure 2).
text.formatted: The framework also incorporates repeated sessions and trajectories for the three dimensions (Figure <ref type="figure">2</ref>).

text.text: Repeated measurements can be scheduled across a predefined period, with timing aligned to academic demands and support delivery.
Longitudinal interpretation should retain continuous measurements, uncertainty, and data-quality indicators rather than relying solely on changes between colours.
Support should address needs established through review, which might include workload adjustments, study support, or referral to appropriate professionals.
Evaluation should begin with feasibility and measurement quality.
Researchers should establish whether students understand and tolerate the tasks, whether usable recordings can be obtained in institutions, and whether repeated scores are sufficiently reliable.
Validation should reflect each intended educational population, including middle-school and high-school students as well as college and university students.
Task demands, reference values, and interpretation require age-appropriate developmental validation.
Task accessibility, language, prior task experience, and neurodevelopmental differences should be considered in design and analysis.
The protocol should document device configuration, sensor placement, task timing, preprocessing, motion handling, and criteria for rejecting inadequate recordings.
Methods for accounting for superficial and systemic contributions should be specified.
Sleep, recent activity, medication, and testing conditions should be recorded where relevant.
Physiological recordings provide an objective source of information, but interpretation must account for the multiple influences on the signal.
Systemic and superficial physiological changes can contribute to fNIRS recordings (Tachtsidis & Scholkmann, 2016), and a stress-related profile is not itself a clinical diagnosis.
text.formatted: Systemic and superficial physiological changes can contribute to fNIRS recordings <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Tachtsidis & Scholkmann, 2016)</ref>, and a stress-related profile is not itself a clinical diagnosis.

text.text: Construct validation should test the proposed dimensions against independent measures and determine whether they are distinguishable.
Comparisons might include validated measures of perceived stress and test anxiety, recovery-related experience, and independently assessed functioning.
No single comparator should be assumed to provide an infallible reference standard for "stress."
Validation of the two-tier pathway must include students across all Tier 1 categories.
Assessing only red-category students would leave the system's missed cases largely unexamined.
Researchers should preregister follow-up criteria and assess whether Tier 2 adds information beyond Tier 1 and routine institutional data.
Algorithms and thresholds should then be tested in independent students and institutions, with subgroup performance and uncertainty reported.
Educational utility requires a further study.
A prospective controlled evaluation should compare the two-tier pathway with a clearly defined existing support pathway.

Outcomes should include whether the pathway identifies independently confirmed difficulties before ordinary referral, how quickly students receive appropriate support, and whether functioning subsequently improves.
Attendance and independently measured learning outcomes can assess educational consequences.
Claims of prevention require evidence of fewer subsequent adverse outcomes relative to the comparison pathway, alongside assessment of unnecessary referrals and missed difficulties.
Examination results should be interpreted alongside prior attainment and relevant contextual factors.
A change in an NPRO-8 score would not, on its own, demonstrate educational benefit.
Targeting physiological assessment may reduce the number of sensor sessions compared with assessing every student.
That arithmetic does not establish savings compared with existing practice.
An economic evaluation should count screening administration, equipment, staffing, follow-up, and downstream services, then relate these costs to demonstrated outcomes.

Participation should involve clear information and informed consent, with additional assent and parental-permission procedures where minors are included, and a clear explanation of how results will be used.
Institutions should separate support information from grading, admissions, and disciplinary decisions.
Reports should describe measurement uncertainty and avoid fixed labels about a student's ability or mental health.
Access to individual records should be limited to those responsible for agreed support; institution-level reporting should protect students from identification in small groups.
Acceptability is part of effectiveness.
Students should be able to decline physiological assessment without losing access to help.
Researchers should examine whether the pathway reaches students equitably and whether it creates additional anxiety, stigma, or inappropriate referrals.
Screening should only be introduced alongside sufficient capacity to respond to the needs it identifies.
Student support should include opportunities for early identification before a request for help, visible deterioration, or crisis becomes the trigger for action.

NPRO-8 Core proposes a new approach to objective assessment within such a proactive pathway: broad student screening, targeted measurement of stress-related load, recovery, and cognitive functioning, and repeated review linked to support.
The preventive ambition is to recognize emerging difficulties early enough to act.
Demonstrating that this approach achieves earlier detection and better student outcomes is the central task for empirical evaluation.
Illustrative reporting across eight sessions for Stress Load, Recovery Capacity, and Functional Impact.
The display shows how an individual trajectory and comparison with baseline could be presented.
Values, colour categories, and improvement labels are examples, not student study results or evidence of intervention benefit.
The Recovery Capacity panel uses concern-state coding, with green indicating a favourable state, rather than a raw capacity scale.
